bodies: United Motor Works latest coup is a single tender award for the supply. of 102 units 3 ton diesel driven forklift trucks and ten units 2’ ton battery forklifts to PSA. These forklifts are now operating
at PSA’s new gateway at Pasir Panjang, Singapore. Quite apart from this deal Toyota forklift trucks are currently the largest selling range of material handling equipment in Singapore and Malaysia.

Their range of forklifts available covers 1000 kg to 25000 kg diesel driven forklift trucks, petrol and LP. gas trucks from 700 kg to 6000 kg and battery powered from 500 kg to 4000 kg. The main models are available almost immediately. Forklift trucks have made material handling fast, efficient and indeed safe. With international trade growing and material handling becomingmore than just efficient and neat stacking, forklifts have undergone many innovations in adaptability.

The Toyota forklifts come with many attachments suitable for various diversified industries. For very high lifts a 3-stage mast can be fitted to reach a height of 6500 mm (256”). To load and unload in low holds of ships and containers a 2stage full free lift mast can be attached together with a side-shifter. Their forklifts can also be attached with clamps for work with bales of cotton or pulp, drums and a full 360 rotating clamp for paper rolls. Further versatility of these workhorses is obtained by attaching a ram for coiled goods, a crane arm for lifting objects with slings, hinged forks which can be coupled with bucket, load stabilizers for high stack and fragile cargo. Toyota forklifts come with UMW after sales service guarantee. UMW maintain a large fleet of mobile inspection and service vehicles manned by highly skilled trouble-shooter mechanics. This unit minimises lay down time and regularly inspects Toyota forklifts at worksites to diagnose potential problems free of charge, advise on necessary replacement parts and service the trucks if required. They are on call as well. One UMW spokesman added, “Our motto is — service with expertise.” A mouthful? No, a varifiable fact.

8bdeda19-db38-4a93-9b64-4d5e56b09f62.title: CONTAINERISED PLEASURE BOATS
bodies: Newly-built pleasure boats are becoming a common sight on the decks of containerships these days, as the box carriers are proving a safer and faster mode of transport for high-value cargoes. With the systematic loading and unloading and placement of containers on board, uncontainerisable deck cargoes are not so prone to hard knocks that are common in conventional shipping. American Marine, builder of the Grand Banks range of luxury crafts, over the weekend exported a 32 foot model to a client in Europe. The boat was fixed with a cradle and loaded on board the ScanDutch containership Nedlloyd Delft for a slightly over 20-day trip to Denmark. American Marine, which exports about 10 per cent of its boats to Europe, uses containership transport to ensure the high quality finishing of its crafts remains intact when delivered to customers.

bodies: At the East Lagoon on the northern side of the PSA container terminal , two new container berths are now under construction. These berths will cater increased container traffic expected in the next few years. The first berth will provide a special shore based ramp designed to service the three new vessels of the ANRO Consortium which comprises the Australian National Line, Neptune Orient Lines of Singapore, Australia Straits Container Line and Nedllyod Lines. Completion of the berth is expected by the end of September 1977.

The two berths totalling about S$66 million will be 640 metres in length with two main access bridges linking them to a 19.5 hectare marshalling yard and 10.5 heotares of back up land. The schedule was 18 months for completion of the first berth and 26 months for the complete project. To date the schedule has been maintained. Although the extra capacity provided by the 2 berths will help equip the terminal to cater for the estimated growth in container traffic between now and 1980, the project has been designed to be as flexible as possible. Four 35 tonne portainer cranes purchased at a cost of about $$2.56 million each, plus several transtainer cranes will service the berths. This equipment combined with the modern gear and design of the vessels will help cater for the growth in cargo traffic by improving turn-around times and collection and delivery of cargo. The two new berths will be equipped and fully operational by 1979 just about the same time the existing facilities will have reached their optimum capacity. The construction of the two new berths coincides with the commencement of work on a $$50 million inland container depot at Bukit Timah, about 25 kilometres from the terminal. Its function will be a container storage area and a break bulk consolidation depot.

bodies: A RELIABLE and economic method of on-stream analysis for increasing the efficiency of mineral processing is offered by the Australian Mineral Development Laboratories (AMDEL). AMDEL is a contract research organisation providing technical development and consulting services to industry and government in the fields of mineral and material sciences. ‘The on-stream analytical system, using radioisotope immersion probes, has application to heavy metal processing for elements above titanium in the Periodic Table, in larger-scale modern plant. It provides a method of-continuous automatic readout of metal values in process slurry streams, enabling the most efficient operation of mineral processing plant. The highly significant break-through in this new method of analysis has been the Australian development of a range of immersible probes, each housing a detector head assembly, a scintillation counter and a radioisotope source . The probes are designed to measure mineral content and slurry density, with an accuracy practical to the application, using both X-ray fluorescence and X-ray gammaray absorption techniques, while actually immersed in the Process streams. _ The probes aré inexpensive, of rugged construction and easy to install and to replace. Components of the on-stream analytical system are designed and manufactured by AMDEL will research and development support from the Australian Atomic Energy Commission. The Australian Mineral Industry Research Association and the Zinc Corporation. Under the terms of a worldwide agreement, AMDEL carries out the necessary feasibility studies, and designs, manufactures and installs the equipment. The system is sufficiently flexible to allow step-bystep growth from a basic analysis arrangement to one involving fully computerised plant control with feedback from a number of points in the process. Because of this flexibility, the cost of the installation can be effectively controlled to suit the size of the plant. The cost of the equipment, although a half to a third that of competitors, is likely to be about $A113,000 fora typical 3-stream installation. The IOSA immersion probe system has now a proved history of operation for more than five years in Australia and abroad, for copper, lead, zinc, nickel and tin. AMDEL’s services and facilities include: Analytical chemistry, mineralogy, petrology, geochemistry, geochronology, materials technology, ‘operations research, computer services, geostatistics, mine planning, mineral engineering, chemical metallugry, instrumentation, water treatment, process development, feasibility studies, pat design and commissioning. bodies: ASEA, the Swedish worldwide manufacturer of electrical and mechanical equipment, is working on the development of a process using hot isostatic pressing for the safe containment and storage of nuclear waste. This development work which is being carried out at the Company’s High-Pressure Laboratory at Robertsfors, in the north of Sweden, promises to contain all dangers in the disposal of nuclear waste. Under high pressure the waste is compacted together to form a dense and solid body which is harder than any kind of rock including granite! this process which is called hot isostatic pressing, is already been used in some of ASEA’s products, for instance, the Quintus Presses marketed throughout the world including Singapore. This new method will not only interest countries who are now grappling with the nuclear waste problem, but also others like the Republic who are seriously considering nuclear energy as an alternative power to oil. ASEA has been working in the field of highpressure research since the 1940s and has developed a number of processes and products which have led to important breakthroughts in materials technology.

CHOOSING THE RIGHT SYSTEM FOR THE BEST PROTECTION For both the shipowner and the shipbuilder the choice of a good paint protection scheme is becoming increasingly important as the prices of steel and labour rise. Ships are becoming more specialised and as a consequence more costly, therefore it is important that shipowners and builders consult their paint supplier before deciding on a system. CONVENTIONAL PAINTS There are many types of paint to choose from; the normal types are Epoxy, Vinyl, Chlorinated Rubber and the so-called conventional. Conventional paints are modernised formulations of the marine paints that have been in existence for many years and invariably consist of primers based on bitumen together with aluminium for underwater surfaces, red lead and zinc chromates for surfaces above water. These primers consist of inorganic pigments which provide good anticorrosive properties to protect your steel. However, a minimum of two coats and preferably three should be applied to obtain the best protection. The primers can be overcoated with antifouling underwater and gloss finishes above water. GRIT BLASTING Before using a Chlorinated Rubber, Epoxy or Vinyl scheme the steel should be grit blasted to Swedish Standard SA2¥%. Immediately after blasting, a coat of Epoxy Blast Primer should be applied. The use of a wash or etch primer based on polyvinylbutyrate is not recommended for the underwater areas and for cargo tanks as they have a tendency to give poor adhesion, once the ship is in service, when used in conjunction with cathodic protection. This will cause an eventual blisting of the subsequent paint system. CHLORINATED RUBBER PAINTS Today there is a great tendency to use Chlorinated Rubber paints, most of which are based on “Alloprene”’, a raw material produced by ICI Mond Division. Chlorinated Rubber (CR) paints incorporate many of the good points of the conventional products, i.e. they include the use of anti-corrosive pigments, but are bonded by a resin containing chlorinated rubber, which is much tougher than the conventional type. CR paints perform extremely well in conjunction with cathodic protection, being able to withstand a greater voltage potential than conventional paints. bodies: The Managing Director of Swift Electronic Engineers, Mr Charlie Hoon, feels that there is an overall shortage of experienced technicians in the marine electronics field. He said, “There is no shortage of lettered technicians, by this I mean technicians who have completed technical school or even college courses. But what the marine electronics industry needs, and urgently, is technicians who have practical experience and are willing to go on acquiring skills.”’ Mr Hoon feels that while it is good to have theoretical knowledge it should not be forgotten that the technician is required at a work site on a piece of equipment and not with a pen and paper in his hands. “College graduates must think of themselves as technicians first and administrators second. It is only after knowing what is happening at the grease-pot level that an academically qualified technician can become an administrator fit to give instructions,” the Managing Director continued. Work in any kind of engineering establishment, particularly in the marine field, has rather odd working hours, but it is rather unfortunate that a lot of technical employees in these organisations prefer to keep to fixed working hours. Swift Electronic Engineers, which employs a large number of specialised marine electronics technicians is perhaps the only company in Singapore which can repair gyro-compasses. The company has had to send several of its staff to Japan and the United States of America for basic and advanced training in the maintenance and repair of various brands in radar, single-sideband radio-telephone, VHF, transmitters and receivers, and echo sounders. They carry a very wide range of spare parts and offer twenty-four hour service. “There have been occasions when we have been so short of technical staff that I’ve had to attend to repair and installation jobs myself,” said Mr Hoon who holds A.LP.R.E. and 2nd class P.M.G. annotations.text: Qualified Marine Electronics Technicians Shortage

The Managing Director of Swift Electronic Engineers, Mr Charlie Hoon, feels that there is an overall shortage of experienced technicians in the marine electronics field. He said, “There is no shortage of lettered technicians, by this I mean technicians who have completed technical school or even college courses. But what the marine electronics industry needs, and urgently, is technicians who have practical experience and are willing to go on acquiring skills.”’ Mr Hoon feels that while it is good to have theoretical knowledge it should not be forgotten that the technician is required at a work site on a piece of equipment and not with a pen and paper in his hands. “College graduates must think of themselves as technicians first and administrators second. It is only after knowing what is happening at the grease-pot level that an academically qualified technician can become an administrator fit to give instructions,” the Managing Director continued. Work in any kind of engineering establishment, particularly in the marine field, has rather odd working hours, but it is rather unfortunate that a lot of technical employees in these organisations prefer to keep to fixed working hours. Swift Electronic Engineers, which employs a large number of specialised marine electronics technicians is perhaps the only company in Singapore which can repair gyro-compasses. The company has had to send several of its staff to Japan and the United States of America for basic and advanced training in the maintenance and repair of various brands in radar, single-sideband radio-telephone, VHF, transmitters and receivers, and echo sounders. They carry a very wide range of spare parts and offer twenty-four hour service. “There have been occasions when we have been so short of technical staff that I’ve had to attend to repair and installation jobs myself,” said Mr Hoon who holds A.LP.R.E. and 2nd class P.M.G. Swift Electronic Engineers were given the task to install a whole radio room on board the “Golden Season’ belonging to Guan Guan Shipping and the ‘Kota Tanjong” belonging to Pacific International Line. The company has the following subsidiaries, UNI Swift Engineering offering services in motors, generators, winches and pumps, ship’s electrical wiring and marine engine repairs. Lybron (S) Pte Ltd, is the sole agent for Sonneborn Chemstruction Systems of USA, and UCO Swift Engineering Ltd, — “the only local radio company to have an operational office in Bahrain,” the Managing Director said proudly. “The chances of the shipping industry picking up in Singapore are good, but it will take time. Our main market at the moment is Indonesia but later developments can change this situation,” Mr Charlie Hoon concluded.

The basic concept of the heat absorber is nothing new. What is new and good is that the Singapore version is manufactured and assembled in Singapore by a Singaporean. This would make it cheaper all round and maintenance only as far as a telephone. The heat absorber, as the name implies, absorbs radiation heat of the sun to heat the water in its maze of copper piping and plates. An insulated storage tank connected to power supply as well, for sunless periods, maintains the temperature of the heated water. The tank can hold up to 40 gallons of heated water which is just about sufficient for four people to have a shower individually or other wise — remember the energy crisis cartoons of not so long ago? Theoretically the idea is simple — have sun will have hot water — but the actual application is nothing short of a jungle of mathematical formulae. Nonetheless, this is a piece of engineering worth-installing not only in homes but in industries requiring constant and cheap supply of hot water. The equipment is assembled at Equatorial Engineering and installed on site. Actual installation takes only a few days. Ask Farid about it. He is a pleasant man to talk to.

Putting solar heat energy to work has become virtually a mania and many an engineer have put forward many ideas, particularly in the field of solar heat energy storage. Oil is, however still available, albeit expensive with its many storms in a teacup. Energy as such has become a burning issue and the average man is made to pay heavily. This has led to the proliferation of ideas on how to cut down costs on at least domestic electricity bills. The brightest and the most workable solution, at least in part, is to install heat absorbers on house roofs. These heat absorbers provide instant hot water (180 _F) without going through electric water heaters. There is hot water in the kitchen and bathroom and elsewhere if you need it and the authorities are happy you are saving energy. Your pocket is that much richer because you are paying less on electricity. And where do you get this heat absorber? In Singapore, made in Singapore, from R Farid who manufactures, installs and maintains it. Mr Farid is an engineer whose stock-in-trade is refrigeration, air-conditioning and allied services in ships. He is the Technical Director of Equatorial Engineering Pte Limited. In his spare time, Mr Farid developed various component parts of the heat absorber, tested it and had one installed in his home seven years ago — it worked and he saved is still saving. Presently, he is installing a unit in a lovely home in one of the more exclusive housing estates. The owner sounded very enthusiatic about it. Who would not with the prospect of saving money.

At the East Lagoon on the northern side of the PSA container terminal , two new container berths are now under construction. The two berths totalling about S$66 million will be 640 metres in length with two main access bridges linking them to a 19.5 hectare marshalling yard and 10.5 heotares of back up land. The two new berths will be equipped and fully operational by 1979 just about the same time the existing facilities will have reached their optimum capacity. The construction of the two new berths coincides with the commencement of work on a $$50 million inland container depot at Bukit Timah, about 25 kilometres from the terminal. A RELIABLE and economic method of on-stream analysis for increasing the efficiency of mineral processing is offered by the Australian Mineral Development Laboratories (AMDEL). AMDEL is a contract research organisation providing technical development and consulting services to industry and government in the fields of mineral and material sciences. ‘The on-stream analytical system, using radioisotope immersion probes, has application to heavy metal processing for elements above titanium in the Periodic Table, in larger-scale modern plant. It provides a method of-continuous automatic readout of metal values in process slurry streams, enabling the most efficient operation of mineral processing plant. The highly significant break-through in this new method of analysis has been the Australian development of a range of immersible probes, each housing a detector head assembly, a scintillation counter and a radioisotope source . The probes are designed to measure mineral content and slurry density, with an accuracy practical to the application, using both X-ray fluorescence and X-ray gammaray absorption techniques, while actually immersed in the Process streams. _ The probes aré inexpensive, of rugged construction and easy to install and to replace. Components of the on-stream analytical system are designed and manufactured by AMDEL will research and development support from the Australian Atomic Energy Commission. The Australian Mineral Industry Research Association and the Zinc Corporation. Under the terms of a worldwide agreement, AMDEL carries out the necessary feasibility studies, and designs, manufactures and installs the equipment. The system is sufficiently flexible to allow step-bystep growth from a basic analysis arrangement to one involving fully computerised plant control with feedback from a number of points in the process. Because of this flexibility, the cost of the installation can be effectively controlled to suit the size of the plant. The cost of the equipment, although a half to a third that of competitors, is likely to be about $A113,000 fora typical 3-stream installation. The IOSA immersion probe system has now a proved history of operation for more than five years in Australia and abroad, for copper, lead, zinc, nickel and tin. AMDEL’s services and facilities include: Analytical chemistry, mineralogy, petrology, geochemistry, geochronology, materials technology, ‘operations research, computer services, geostatistics, mine planning, mineral engineering, chemical metallugry, instrumentation, water treatment, process development, feasibility studies, pat design and commissioning. The world’s first LASH (Lighter Aboard Ship) operator today operates the world’s largest LASH fleet. Central Gulf Lines pioneered LASH operations, beginning in 1969 with the the world’s first LASH vessel, M/V ACADIA FOREST, and adding a sister ship, M/V ATLANTIC FOREST, in 1970. Both of these 860-foot-long, 46, 500-ton, 83 LASH barge-capacity vessels serve U.S. Gulf ports, UK/North Europe and the Middle East. The. company’s LASH system demonstrated cargo shipper and operational advantages both for areas that contain back-up inland river systems, as well as for major and developing port areas that are not connected to such inland systems. Initial operating experience proved the soundness and versatility of LASH as an effective transportation system, and Central Gulf proceeded with a $120 million fleet expansion program that encompassed

the building of three LASH vessels and more than 600 LASH barges. These new LASH vessels, S.S. GREEN VALLEY, GREEN HARBOUR and GREEN ISLAND inaugurated in late 1974 the first LASH service to Singapore, Indonesia, Malaysia and other South East Asian points, serving U.S. Gulf and East coast ports outbound and inbound. Sailings every 25 days were established, resulting in positive acceptance by exporters and importers. Largest cargoliners of their type, the vessels carry 89 LASH barges, are 893 feet long, have a service speed of 22 knots and a deadweight of 46,039 tons. Central Gulf’s world-leading LASH barge fleet now numbers 1,430 units. In addition, the company has developed and operates four float-on/ float-off barge feeder vessels called FLASH. The FLASH carriers are shallow-draft vessels that carry from eight to 15 LASH barges to and from

ports that cannot accommodate oceangoing liners and that were formerly served only by indirect means involving numerous transhipments of cargo. The FLASH vessels are towed by seagoing towboats between the LASH ocean carrier that calls major ports and the many outlying ports that Central Gulf serves. Central Gulf re-entered the Middle East trade in the fall of 1975, offering LASH service regularly from U.S. Gulf and East coast ports to ports in the Red Sea and Arabian-Persian Gulf. Today, Central Gulf operates seven LASH vessels on regularlyscheduled sailings to the Middle East, while continuing to maintain its established service commitments to the United Kingdom, Europe and South East Asia. Central Gulf heads up the corporation’s Ocean Shipping Group. The affiliation with Trans Union has enabled Central Gulf Lines to proceed with plans for continued growth and expansion of its fleet, while providing for continuation and broadening of comprehensive transportation services for firms engaged in foreign trade. A RELIABLE and economic method of on-stream analysis for increasing the efficiency of mineral processing is offered by the Australian Mineral Development Laboratories (AMDEL). AMDEL is a contract research organisation providing technical development and consulting services to industry and government in the fields of mineral and material sciences. ‘The on-stream analytical system, using radioisotope immersion probes, has application to heavy metal processing for elements above titanium in the Periodic Table, in larger-scale modern plant. It provides a method of-continuous automatic readout of metal values in process slurry streams, enabling the most efficient operation of mineral processing plant. The highly significant break-through in this new method of analysis has been the Australian development of a range of immersible probes, each housing a detector head assembly, a scintillation counter and a radioisotope source . The probes are designed to measure mineral content and slurry density, with an accuracy practical to the application, using both X-ray fluorescence and X-ray gammaray absorption techniques, while actually immersed in the Process streams. _ The probes aré inexpensive, of rugged construction and easy to install and to replace. Components of the on-stream analytical system are designed and manufactured by AMDEL will research and development support from the Australian Atomic Energy Commission. The Australian Mineral Industry Research Association and the Zinc Corporation. Under the terms of a worldwide agreement, AMDEL carries out the necessary feasibility studies, and designs, manufactures and installs the equipment. The system is sufficiently flexible to allow step-bystep growth from a basic analysis arrangement to one involving fully computerised plant control with feedback from a number of points in the process. Because of this flexibility, the cost of the installation can be effectively controlled to suit the size of the plant. The cost of the equipment, although a half to a third that of competitors, is likely to be about $A113,000 fora typical 3-stream installation. The IOSA immersion probe system has now a proved history of operation for more than five years in Australia and abroad, for copper, lead, zinc, nickel and tin. CHOOSING THE RIGHT SYSTEM FOR THE BEST PROTECTION For both the shipowner and the shipbuilder the choice of a good paint protection scheme is becoming increasingly important as the prices of steel and labour rise. Ships are becoming more specialised and as a consequence more costly, therefore it is important that shipowners and builders consult their paint supplier before deciding on a system. CONVENTIONAL PAINTS There are many types of paint to choose from; the normal types are Epoxy, Vinyl, Chlorinated Rubber and the so-called conventional. Conventional paints are modernised formulations of the marine paints that have been in existence for many years and invariably consist of primers based on bitumen together with aluminium for underwater surfaces, red lead and zinc chromates for surfaces above water. These primers consist of inorganic pigments which provide good anticorrosive properties to protect your steel. However, a minimum of two coats and preferably three should be applied to obtain the best protection. The primers can be overcoated with antifouling underwater and gloss finishes above water. GRIT BLASTING Before using a Chlorinated Rubber, Epoxy or Vinyl scheme the steel should be grit blasted to Swedish Standard SA2¥%. Immediately after blasting, a coat of Epoxy Blast Primer should be applied. The use of a wash or etch primer based on polyvinylbutyrate is not recommended for the underwater areas and for cargo tanks as they have a tendency to give poor adhesion, once the ship is in service, when used in conjunction with cathodic protection. This will cause an eventual blisting of the subsequent paint system. CHLORINATED RUBBER PAINTS Today there is a great tendency to use Chlorinated Rubber paints, most of which are based on “Alloprene”’, a raw material produced by ICI Mond Division. Chlorinated Rubber (CR) paints incorporate many of the good points of the conventional products, i.e. they include the use of anti-corrosive pigments, but are bonded by a resin containing chlorinated rubber, which is much tougher than the conventional type. CR paints perform extremely well in conjunction with cathodic protection, being able to withstand a greater voltage potential than conventional paints. The Managing Director of Swift Electronic Engineers, Mr Charlie Hoon, feels that there is an overall shortage of experienced technicians in the marine electronics field. He said, “There is no shortage of lettered technicians, by this I mean technicians who have completed technical school or even college courses. But what the marine electronics industry needs, and urgently, is technicians who have practical experience and are willing to go on acquiring skills.”’ Mr Hoon feels that while it is good to have theoretical knowledge it should not be forgotten that the technician is required at a work site on a piece of equipment and not with a pen and paper in his hands. “College graduates must think of themselves as technicians first and administrators second. It is only after knowing what is happening at the grease-pot level that an academically qualified technician can become an administrator fit to give instructions,” the Managing Director continued. Work in any kind of engineering establishment, particularly in the marine field, has rather odd working hours, but it is rather unfortunate that a lot of technical employees in these organisations prefer to keep to fixed working hours. Swift Electronic Engineers, which employs a large number of specialised marine electronics technicians is perhaps the only company in Singapore which can repair gyro-compasses. The company has had to send several of its staff to Japan and the United States of America for basic and advanced training in the maintenance and repair of various brands in radar, single-sideband radio-telephone, VHF, transmitters and receivers, and echo sounders. They carry a very wide range of spare parts and offer twenty-four hour service. “There have been occasions when we have been so short of technical staff that I’ve had to attend to repair and installation jobs myself,” said Mr Hoon who holds A.LP.R.E. and 2nd class P.M.G. Swift Electronic Engineers were given the task to install a whole radio room on board the “Golden Season’ belonging to Guan Guan Shipping and the ‘Kota Tanjong” belonging to Pacific International Line. The company has the following subsidiaries, UNI Swift Engineering offering services in motors, generators, winches and pumps, ship’s electrical wiring and marine engine repairs. Lybron (S) Pte Ltd, is the sole agent for Sonneborn Chemstruction Systems of USA, and UCO Swift Engineering Ltd, — “the only local radio company to have an operational office in Bahrain,” the Managing Director said proudly. “The chances of the shipping industry picking up in Singapore are good, but it will take time. A new form of protection is offered to crews on offshore drilling rigs in the event of disaster at sea. Whittaker Corporation of California USA, has introduced a diesel-powered, 50-man survival capsule capable of getaway speeds of more than six knots. Shaped like an elongated flying saucer, the Whittaker capsule is powered by a Perkins 4.15 marine diesel engine, a four-cylinder, in-line unit that develops 62 horsepower. The capsule measures 6 meters long, 3.16 meters high and 4.27 meters wide. Fully loaded with people and provisions, it weighs approximately 7.7 metric tons. The Perkins 4.154 diesel installed in the 50-man capsule is hydraulically started, and colling is achieved by a seawater-freshwater heat exchanger. Standard equipment includes a 12-volt, 42 ampere alternator with a solid-state integral regulator, along with oil pressure indicator light, charge indicator light, and temperature gauge. An engine-driven pump supplied a sprinkler system with raw water at a rate of 125 gallons per minute.

Money is important for the private investigator to survive but a good majority of them earn it through honest and dedicated service. It would be interesting to hear comments on “Industrial Security” from readers and the private investigators.

Rapid industrialisation, in any country, leaves in its wake many ill effects. These lead to the necessity for increased surveillance. In Singapore, of late, there has been an increase in the number of companies specialising in industrial security but also in private investigations. Many of these firms have chalked up remarkable successes in not only preventing crimes, as it were, but also bringing to justice culprits after an offence had been committed. A private investigator, who declined to be named, we spoke to said, “Its amazing that a lot of companies in Singapore do not bother to check on the background of applicants for top positions. In my opinion checks should be made before employment and for promotional purposes. Mind you, I am not saying that all applicants etc, are dishonest, but what if you have hired one? Food for thought this. It would appear,that the old adage “prevention is better than cure” is the clue to solving this ever present inconvenience and embarrassment. No reputable company likes its name to be bandied around in the courts of law for want of better care. There are countless crimes being committed by employees in just about every firm. Some of the common ones are kickbacks, pilferage and outright hand-in-gloves at thievery and robbery. All this can be minimised at least, if not, stopped, if only a little more care and attention were paid to security. Not yet rampant but beginning to loom its head in Singapore is industrial espionage which takes the form of counterfeit at the moment. Prone to this are mainly consumer products. But it is not uncommon to find trade marks and patents being infringed. The legal process to disentangle from these is expensive, product-wise damaging, time-consum- “yg and embarrassing to say the least. Admittedly, it is not easy to avoid trademark and patent infringements but expert advice from security and other allied counsultants would reduce the tisk. This again is, perhaps, where private investigators can be of service. Mr W D Anthony, a private investigator and security expert himself said, “A consultant should be a person who can give unbiased, unprejudiced advice entirely to the benefit of the client.” Private investigators charge according to the advice given. However, there are always those who are unscrupulous in every trade.

The basic concept of the heat absorber is nothing new. What is new and good is that the Singapore version is manufactured and assembled in Singapore by a Singaporean. This would make it cheaper all round and maintenance only as far as a telephone. The heat absorber, as the name implies, absorbs radiation heat of the sun to heat the water in its maze of copper piping and plates. An insulated storage tank connected to power supply as well, for sunless periods, maintains the temperature of the heated water. The tank can hold up to 40 gallons of heated water which is just about sufficient for four people to have a shower individually or other wise — remember the energy crisis cartoons of not so long ago? Theoretically the idea is simple — have sun will have hot water — but the actual application is nothing short of a jungle of mathematical formulae. Nonetheless, this is a piece of engineering worth-installing not only in homes but in industries requiring constant and cheap supply of hot water. The equipment is assembled at Equatorial Engineering and installed on site. Actual installation takes only a few days. Ask Farid about it. He is a pleasant man to talk to.

Putting solar heat energy to work has become virtually a mania and many an engineer have put forward many ideas, particularly in the field of solar heat energy storage. Oil is, however still available, albeit expensive with its many storms in a teacup. Energy as such has become a burning issue and the average man is made to pay heavily. This has led to the proliferation of ideas on how to cut down costs on at least domestic electricity bills. The brightest and the most workable solution, at least in part, is to install heat absorbers on house roofs. These heat absorbers provide instant hot water (180 _F) without going through electric water heaters. There is hot water in the kitchen and bathroom and elsewhere if you need it and the authorities are happy you are saving energy. Your pocket is that much richer because you are paying less on electricity. And where do you get this heat absorber? In Singapore, made in Singapore, from R Farid who manufactures, installs and maintains it. Mr Farid is an engineer whose stock-in-trade is refrigeration, air-conditioning and allied services in ships. He is the Technical Director of Equatorial Engineering Pte Limited. In his spare time, Mr Farid developed various component parts of the heat absorber, tested it and had one installed in his home seven years ago — it worked and he saved is still saving. Presently, he is installing a unit in a lovely home in one of the more exclusive housing estates. The owner sounded very enthusiatic about it. Who would not with the prospect of saving money.
